title: The map maker
text:
When Arif was eleven, his grandfather gave him an old brass compass. "A map-maker never gets lost," he said, "because he writes down every step of the way." Arif did not understand then. He understood now.

The class trip to the highlands had started well. The group, led by Mr Hartono, followed a path through a pine forest. Arif lagged behind, drawing a map in his notebook: a stream here, a fallen tree there, a hill shaped like a sleeping buffalo. Mist began to creep between the trunks.

By the time Arif looked up, he could no longer see his classmates. "Hello?" he called. His voice was swallowed by the fog. He felt the old familiar cold in his stomach, the feeling he got when a test paper landed on his desk. Panic whispered in his ear: Run! Go anywhere! Just go!

Instead, Arif sat on a rock and took three long breaths. "Think," he told himself. He opened his notebook. The map showed the stream, the fallen tree, and the buffalo hill, with arrows in his own handwriting. He placed the compass flat on his palm. The needle trembled, then settled.

Slowly, he began to retrace his path, matching each landmark with its sketch. The stream gurgled where he had drawn it. The fallen tree lay across the path like a sleeping giant. Twice he doubted himself and paused, but each time the notebook proved him right.

Just as the light began to fade, he heard faint voices. "Arif! Arif!" Mr Hartono's torch cut through the mist. Arif ran towards it and the teacher pulled him into a firm, relieved hug.

"How did you find us?" asked Mr Hartono.

Arif held up the notebook. "I didn't," he said, his voice cracking with a smile. "My map found me."

That night, in the warm light of the camp fire, Arif wrote a new line at the top of his map: Always write down the way.
